title: Getting Past No: Negotiating in Difficult Situations
author: William Ury
summary:
Getting Past No is William Ury's answer to the question he says he was asked more than any other after co-writing Getting to Yes: what do you do when the other side simply won't cooperate? Where the earlier book focused on principled negotiation between reasonably willing parties, this one is built specifically for negotiating with people who are angry, entrenched, deceptive, or simply uninterested in a joint solution — a stubborn boss, a hostile counterpart, an intransigent bureaucracy, or an outright adversary.

Ury frames the challenge around five distinct barriers that block cooperative negotiation: your own reactive impulses under stress, the other side's negative emotions, their tendency to dig into a fixed position, their underlying dissatisfaction with any agreement (often rooted in fear of losing face or the idea simply not being theirs), and their inclination to use power to dominate rather than negotiate. Rather than a single technique, Ury proposes a five-step "breakthrough negotiation" strategy that corresponds directly to these five barriers, built on an idea borrowed from Japanese martial arts: instead of meeting resistance with force, the skilled negotiator goes around it.

Before detailing the five steps, the book opens with a prologue on preparation, arguing that most negotiation outcomes are determined before the conversation even starts — through clarity about your own interests, options, standards, alternatives, and proposal. The five steps that follow — don't react (go to the balcony), don't argue (step to their side), don't reject (reframe), don't push (build a golden bridge), and don't escalate (use power to educate rather than defeat) — each get a full chapter of specific techniques illustrated with real, often high-stakes examples.

The book's most memorable extended illustrations include a detailed salary negotiation walked through step by step, and a forty-seven-hour hostage standoff at a New York hospital in which a detective successfully applied breakthrough principles to secure the release of hostages unharmed. Ury closes with the parable of seventeen camels that cannot be divided among three sons until a wise woman lends an eighteenth camel to make the math work — a metaphor for how the breakthrough strategy itself often functions as the "extra" element that makes an otherwise intractable negotiation solvable, without requiring either side to fully capitulate.

sections.title: Prologue: Preparation
sections.summary:
This opening section establishes the book's foundational claim: that negotiation outcomes are largely determined before a conversation begins, through disciplined preparation, and that skipping this step is the single most common cause of failed negotiations.

Ury lays out five specific elements of preparation: interests (what each side truly cares about, beneath their stated position), options (creative possibilities for mutual gain), standards (independent, objective benchmarks like market value or precedent that can be appealed to), alternatives (what you'll do if this negotiation fails), and a concrete proposal to bring to the table. He argues that most people prepare their position but not these underlying elements, leaving them unable to adapt when the conversation doesn't go as expected.

The chapter hands off to the five-step strategy by establishing that preparation isn't a separate task from breakthrough negotiation — it's the foundation the five steps are built on.
keyLessons: Most negotiation outcomes are shaped before the conversation starts, through preparation, not during it.
Preparing your interests, options, standards, alternatives, and a proposal matters more than rehearsing your position.

sections.title: Don't React — Go to the Balcony
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the first barrier — your own reactive impulses — and introduces "going to the balcony" as the practice of mentally stepping back from an escalating exchange to observe it rather than immediately reacting from anger, fear, or the urge to give in.

Ury describes the three typical reactive patterns people fall into under pressure — striking back, giving in, or breaking off the relationship entirely — and argues all three surrender control of the negotiation to the other side's behavior. The "balcony" is presented as a literal pause technique: taking a break, buying time before responding, or simply naming internally what's happening rather than reacting to it immediately.

The chapter closes by connecting self-control to the next step, arguing that a negotiator who can't manage their own reaction has no chance of skillfully addressing the other side's emotions, which the next chapter takes up directly.
keyLessons: Reactive responses under pressure (striking back, giving in, walking away) surrender control of the negotiation to the other side.
Deliberately pausing before responding — "going to the balcony" — restores the ability to choose a strategic response.

sections.title: Don't Argue — Step to Their Side
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the second barrier — the other side's negative emotions — through a counterintuitive move: rather than arguing back or defending your position immediately, the negotiator first disarms the other side by genuinely listening and acknowledging their perspective.

Ury describes specific techniques for this, including active listening, paraphrasing the other side's point back to them accurately, and acknowledging their feelings and their competence without necessarily agreeing with their conclusions. He is explicit that this is not capitulation — acknowledging someone's anger or position is different from accepting it — but argues it reliably lowers defensiveness enough to make the next steps possible.

The chapter transitions to the third step by noting that a disarmed counterpart is now more available to actually reconsider their fixed position, which is the focus of the following chapter.
keyLessons: Genuinely acknowledging the other side's perspective and emotions, without agreeing with their conclusion, reliably lowers defensiveness.
Active listening and accurate paraphrasing are concrete, learnable techniques for "stepping to their side."

sections.title: Don't Reject — Reframe
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the third barrier — the other side's rigid position — by introducing reframing: redirecting the conversation from a battle over fixed positions toward a joint exploration of underlying interests and options, largely through the strategic use of questions rather than direct rebuttal.

Ury offers specific reframing techniques, such as asking "why" or "why not" questions that invite the other side to explain their reasoning rather than simply restating their demand, and asking "what if" questions that introduce new possibilities without requiring either side to formally concede anything yet. He emphasizes that rejecting a position outright tends to entrench it further, while reframing it as a problem to solve together tends to loosen it.

The chapter hands off to the next step by noting that even a successfully reframed conversation still needs to produce an agreement the other side can actually accept, which the "golden bridge" chapter addresses.
keyLessons: Directly rejecting a fixed position tends to entrench it further; reframing it as a shared problem tends to loosen it.
Strategic questions ("why," "what if") redirect conversation toward interests and options without requiring premature concessions.

sections.title: Don't Push — Build a Golden Bridge
sections.summary:
This chapter addresses the fourth barrier — the other side's dissatisfaction with any agreement, often driven by fear of losing face or the proposal simply not being their own idea — by describing how to make an agreement easy, even attractive, for the other side to accept.

Ury argues that people resist agreements imposed on them even when the terms are reasonable, and describes building a "golden bridge" by involving the other party in shaping the solution, satisfying unmet interests they haven't stated directly, helping them save face, and slowing the process down enough that acceptance doesn't feel rushed or coerced. He illustrates this with a detailed salary negotiation example, showing each principle applied in sequence.

The chapter closes by connecting to the final barrier — situations where the other side still believes they can simply win through raw power — which the last chapter addresses.
keyLessons: People resist agreements imposed on them even when the terms are objectively reasonable; involvement in shaping the solution matters as much as the terms themselves.
Helping the other side save face is often a practical requirement for their genuine acceptance of an agreement, not just a courtesy.

sections.title: Don't Escalate — Use Power to Educate
sections.summary:
The final chapter addresses the fifth barrier — a counterpart who believes they can simply dominate through power rather than negotiate — by describing how to use one's own power not to defeat the other side, but to show them that their best alternative to negotiating is genuinely worse than reaching agreement.

Ury distinguishes this from raw escalation or threats, framing it instead as helping the other party accurately see the costs of not negotiating. He illustrates the principle with an extended account of a forty-seven-hour hostage standoff at Kings County Hospital, in which a detective applied breakthrough principles under extreme pressure to secure the release of all hostages unharmed, and closes the book with the parable of the eighteenth camel — a metaphor for how the breakthrough approach itself can be the additional element that makes an apparently unsolvable negotiation solvable.

The book ends without a separate summary chapter, closing instead on Abraham Lincoln's response to a critic who objected to his conciliatory treatment of enemies — reinforcing the book's final message that turning adversaries into partners, rather than defeating them, is the most durable form of victory in negotiation.
keyLessons: Using power to help someone see the true cost of their alternative to negotiating is different from — and more effective than — simply escalating or threatening.
Breakthrough negotiation aims to turn adversaries into negotiating partners rather than to defeat them outright.
Most negotiation outcomes are shaped before the conversation starts, through preparation on interests, options, standards, and alternatives.
Reactive responses under pressure (striking back, giving in, walking away) hand control of the negotiation to the other side.
Genuinely acknowledging the other side's perspective and emotions lowers their defensiveness without requiring you to agree with them.
Directly rejecting a rigid position tends to entrench it further; reframing it as a shared problem loosens it instead.
People resist agreements imposed on them, even reasonable ones; involving them in shaping the solution and helping them save face matters as much as the terms.
Using power to help someone see the true cost of not negotiating differs from — and outperforms — raw escalation or threats.
The goal of breakthrough negotiation is to turn adversaries into negotiating partners, not to defeat them.
Indirect approaches — going around resistance rather than confronting it head-on — succeed more often than direct force in negotiation.

quotes.text: Negotiation is the process of back-and-forth communication aimed at reaching agreement.
There is an alternative: joint problem-solving.
There is no magic recipe that will guarantee your success in every negotiation.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Breakthrough Negotiation (The Five Steps)
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Ury's core framework for negotiating with an uncooperative or difficult counterpart: don't react (go to the balcony), don't argue (step to their side), don't reject (reframe), don't push (build a golden bridge), and don't escalate (use power to educate, not defeat). Each step addresses a specific barrier to joint problem-solving.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Spans the five main chapters of the book

conceptsFrameworks.name: Going to the Balcony
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A self-management technique of mentally or physically stepping back from an escalating exchange to observe it with some distance, rather than immediately reacting from anger, fear, or pressure — restoring the ability to choose a deliberate response.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Don't React — Go to the Balcony

conceptsFrameworks.name: Building a Golden Bridge
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A framework for making an agreement genuinely easy for the other party to accept, by involving them in shaping the solution, satisfying unstated interests, helping them save face, and not rushing acceptance — addressing the common barrier of resistance to any imposed agreement.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Don't Push — Build a Golden Bridge

actionSteps: Before your next difficult conversation, write out your own interests, possible options, objective standards you could appeal to, and your best alternative if no agreement is reached — before rehearsing what you plan to say.
The next time you feel the urge to strike back or immediately concede in a tense exchange, pause and take a break of at least a few minutes before responding — practicing "going to the balcony."
In your next disagreement, before stating your own view, paraphrase the other person's position back to them accurately enough that they agree you've understood it.
When facing a fixed "no," ask a genuine "why" or "what if" question instead of directly rejecting or arguing against their position.
reflectionQuestions: In your current difficult negotiations or conflicts, which of the five barriers (your reaction, their emotion, their position, their dissatisfaction, or their power) is actually the biggest obstacle?
Is there an agreement you're currently pushing that the other person hasn't had any real hand in shaping?
Where have you mistaken escalation for strength in a recent disagreement, when a more indirect approach might have worked better?

points: The book's most dramatic illustration — the Kings County Hospital hostage standoff — is a high-stakes, unusual scenario; readers should be cautious about over-generalizing lessons from crisis/hostage negotiation directly to everyday workplace or personal disputes, which typically differ significantly in stakes and dynamics.

Because the five-step framework is presented as broadly applicable ("diplomats... lawyers... spouses"), it risks understating how differently these principles need to be adapted across vastly different contexts, power dynamics, and cultural negotiating norms.

The book assumes a counterpart who is difficult or entrenched but ultimately capable of being reasoned with; it offers less guidance for negotiating with a party acting in outright bad faith or with no genuine interest in any agreement at all.

As a work of practical negotiation strategy rather than empirical social science, the book's claims rest primarily on Ury's professional experience and illustrative case examples rather than controlled research, which is typical of the genre but worth noting for readers seeking an evidence-based treatment.

whoThisIsFor: Anyone who regularly has to negotiate with a difficult, entrenched, or uncooperative counterpart — in business, legal disputes, or high-stakes personal situations.
whenToReadThis: Before entering a specific negotiation you expect to be contentious, or when a previous approach to a recurring conflict has repeatedly failed to produce movement.

authorBio.name: William Ury
authorBio.bio:
William Ury is an American author, negotiator, and mediator who co-founded Harvard's Program on Negotiation and directs its Global Negotiation Project. He first became widely known as co-author, with Roger Fisher, of *Getting to Yes*, one of the most influential negotiation books ever published, which introduced the framework of principled negotiation.

Over several decades, Ury has worked as a negotiation advisor and mediator in a wide range of high-stakes contexts, including labor disputes, corporate conflicts, and international and civil conflicts, drawing on this practical experience in his subsequent books, including *Getting Past No*, written specifically to address negotiating with uncooperative or adversarial counterparts.

Ury continues to teach, write, and consult on negotiation and conflict resolution, and is regarded as one of the most prominent figures in the modern field of negotiation theory and practice.

Quotes were verified across multiple independent sources and kept to a small set given the copyright-safe limits noted at the top of this file.
